meta.blurb: A Roman statesman tells a younger friend that the only thing we truly own is time, and most of us give it away. The letters of Seneca on fear, grief, friendship and death read like warm, sharp advice from across the table.
meta.bible: Seneca (Lucius Annaeus Seneca): a Roman Stoic philosopher, writer and statesman, born in Corduba in Spain about 4 BCE and raised in Rome; he advised the emperor Nero, stepped back from public life in about 62 CE, and died in 65 CE. Lucilius: a younger friend of Seneca, a Roman official who, it seems, governed Sicily; the letters are addressed to him. Moral Letters (Letters to Lucilius): 124 letters survive, written in the last years of Seneca's life, in plain and friendly Latin. Stoicism: a school of thought founded by Zeno in Athens around 300 BCE, which teaches reason, virtue and a steady mind. Nero: the Roman emperor. Tacitus: a Roman historian who describes Seneca's death. Epicurus: a Greek thinker whom Seneca quotes. Cato: a Roman famous for courage and honesty. Cleanthes: an early Stoic whose lines Seneca translates. Bassus: Aufidius Bassus, an old friend. Metronax: a philosopher whose lectures Seneca attended. Paulina: Seneca's wife. Baiae, Naples, Lyon, Sicily, Spain, Rome, Athens, Egypt, France: places. Saturnalia: a Roman winter festival. Montaigne: a French thinker who admired Seneca. Greek, Latin, Roman, Christian, Renaissance, Middle Ages: terms. Each beat names the letter it comes from. Seneca lived in a society that accepted slavery; this is stated honestly. Voice and tone: warm, clear and thoughtful; practical advice from one friend to another; all facts are real and hedged where uncertain; no gore.

B1B2: Seneca was a Roman thinker and writer who lived about two thousand years ago. In the last years of his life he wrote a long series of letters to a friend about how to live well.
The letters are written to Lucilius, a younger friend of Seneca who worked for the Roman government. Seneca wants them to sound like a quiet talk between two friends, not like a speech.

Seneca belonged to a school of thought called Stoicism, which began in Athens about three hundred years before his time. Stoics believe that we are happiest when we use reason, live well and stay calm.
In the very first letter, Seneca tells Lucilius to claim his time for himself. Much of life passes, he says, while we do nothing or do things that do not matter.
In Letter Two, Seneca warns that a mind which wanders from book to book never settles anywhere. He advises us to choose a few good writers and to read them slowly, until their ideas become our own.

In Letter Three, Seneca gives Lucilius some careful advice about how to choose a true friend. Think carefully before you trust someone, he says, but once you have chosen, give your trust with your whole heart.
Seneca tells Lucilius that fear of death can ruin a whole life, long before death arrives. Philosophy, he says, helps us to look at it calmly, so that we may live without trembling.
In Letter Five, Seneca warns against showing off, even when what we show is philosophy. A wise person should live simply and quietly, so that others are not made uncomfortable by his habits.
In Letter Six, Seneca says that he can feel himself changing for the better. He adds that he would refuse wisdom if he had to keep it secret, because good things are best when shared.
In Letter Seven, Seneca says that he comes home from a crowd feeling worse than when he left. Being among many people, he warns, can slowly teach us their faults, especially at cruel public shows.
In Letter Eight, Seneca explains that he has withdrawn from public life, but not out of laziness. He is writing, he says, for people of later ages, in the hope that his words may help them.
In Letter Nine, Seneca asks whether a wise person needs friends at all. He decides that such a person can stand alone, but still wants friends, because he wants someone to care for.
In Letter Twelve, Seneca visits his old country house and sees that everything, including himself, has grown old. Instead of being sad, he decides to enjoy each day as though it were a complete life.
In Letter Thirteen, Seneca says that we are frightened by more things than can actually hurt us. We suffer far more often in our imagination than we ever do in real life, he adds.
In Letter Sixteen, Seneca says that philosophy is not a clever trick for showing off in public. It is a daily guide that shapes the mind and helps us to live without fear.

In Letter Eighteen, Seneca describes a festival time, when people eat and drink too much. He suggests that Lucilius live on plain food and rough clothes for a few days, to test whether poverty is so terrible.
In Letter Twenty, Seneca says that philosophy teaches us to act, not just to talk. If a person's words and life do not agree, he warns, his teaching is not worth very much.

In Letter Twenty-One, Seneca makes his friend a kind promise about what the future will hold. He tells Lucilius that the letters will carry his name down to future ages, as other famous writers did for their friends.
In Letter Twenty-Three, Seneca says that true joy is a serious matter. It does not depend on money, praise or pleasant events, because it comes from a calm and good mind.
In Letter Twenty-Five, Seneca advises us to choose a wise person as a model and to imagine that he is watching us. This simple trick, he says, can help us to do right, even when we are alone.
In Letter Twenty-Seven, Seneca honestly admits to his friend that he is not yet a wise man. He compares himself to a patient in the same hospital as Lucilius, talking about the illness they share.
In Letter Twenty-Eight, Seneca answers a friend who thinks that travel will cure his sadness. A change of place does not help, he says, because wherever we go, we take our own mind with us.
In Letter Thirty, Seneca describes a recent visit to his old friend Bassus, who is very old and ill. To Seneca's surprise, Bassus is cheerful and talks calmly about death as a natural thing.
In Letter Thirty-Three, Seneca gently asks Lucilius to stop collecting so many famous sayings. A person should not live on borrowed words, he says, but should learn to think and speak for himself.
In Letter Thirty-Eight, Seneca explains that he prefers quiet conversation to grand speeches. Quiet words slip gently into the mind like seeds, he says, and they are more likely to grow there.

In Letter Forty-Seven, Seneca writes about enslaved people, who served in many Roman households. He asks Lucilius to remember that they are human beings, and to treat them as he would like to be treated.
In Letter Fifty-One, Seneca talks about Baiae, a famous seaside resort full of parties and luxury. He chooses not to stay there, because a strong mind needs a place that does not tempt it.
In Letter Fifty-Three, Seneca tells a funny story about a boat trip that made him badly seasick. He laughs at himself, but he also learns that wisdom starts with knowing our weaknesses.

In Letter Fifty-Four, Seneca describes his long illness, which was a kind of asthma that made it hard to breathe. After a bad attack, he says, he felt no fear, because death would be like the time before he was born.

In Letter Fifty-Six, Seneca complains about his rooms, which are right above a public bathhouse. All day he hears grunting athletes, shouting sellers and splashing swimmers, yet he realises that quiet is a matter of the mind.

In Letter Fifty-Seven, Seneca describes a long, dark and dusty tunnel near Naples that gave him a sudden shock. He explains that even a calm person feels such first reactions, and that wisdom lies in what we do next.
In Letter Sixty-Three, Seneca writes to console Lucilius after the death of a dear friend. Tears are natural, he says, but a friend's memory should bring thanks as well as pain.
In Letter Seventy-One, Seneca says that if a sailor does not know his harbour, no wind is the right one. In the same way, a person needs a clear aim in life before he can make good progress.
In Letter Seventy-Six, Seneca says that he is going to a teacher's lectures, even though he is old. Some people laughed at him, but he says it is never too late to learn how to live.
In Letter Seventy-Seven, Seneca watches a fleet of ships arrive and then compares life to a play. It is not how long the play lasts that matters, he says, but how well the actor performs.
In Letter Seventy-Eight, Seneca remembers the long and painful illnesses that he suffered in his own life. He says that a calm mind, good company and happy memories can make pain easier to bear.

In Letter Eighty-Four, Seneca compares good readers to bees, which fly from flower to flower and gather what they need. In the hive they turn it into honey, and we should turn our reading into our own thoughts.
In Letter Ninety-One, Seneca writes about a terrible fire that destroyed much of the city of Lyon. One night, he says, stood between a great city and almost no city at all.
In Letter Ninety-Two, Seneca says that reason is the gift that makes us human. A life guided by reason and goodness, he believes, is the surest way to be happy.
In Letter Ninety-Five, Seneca says that human beings are born to help one another. We are like the stones of an arch, he writes, which would fall down if they did not support each other.

In Letter Ninety-Eight, Seneca warns Lucilius not to be fooled by good fortune, because luck can change at any time. A mind that has already thought about trouble, he says, is hard to shake when trouble comes.
In Letter One Hundred and One, Seneca tells how a friend who seemed perfectly well died very suddenly. Life is uncertain, he says, so we should not put off living well until tomorrow.
In Letter One Hundred and Four, Seneca explains why he looks after his health. His wife Paulina worries about him, and he knows that her life is tied to his.
In Letter One Hundred and Seven, Seneca quotes a short poem by an earlier Stoic. Fate leads the willing, it says, and drags the unwilling, so it is wiser to accept what we cannot change.

In Letter One Hundred and Fifteen, Seneca warns against being dazzled by gold and fine speeches. If we could see a good character with our eyes, he says, we would find it more wonderful than any treasure.
In Letter One Hundred and Nineteen, Seneca argues that nature asks for very little. A person who learns to want only what he needs, he argues, is already rich.
Letter One Hundred and Twenty-Four is the last of Seneca's letters that survives. In it he says that the true good cannot be found by our senses alone, but must be grasped by reason.
In the year 65, the emperor Nero accused Seneca of joining a plot and ordered him to end his life. The historian Tacitus writes that Seneca faced the order calmly and tried to comfort his friends.

Seneca's letters were copied by hand and read all through the Middle Ages, and they were admired again during the Renaissance. Today they are translated into many languages, and many people read them for help with modern worries.
Across all these letters, Seneca asks us to value our time, choose good friends, face our fears and be kind. You do not need to master every lesson, because one small change begun today is enough.
C1C2: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born in Spain around the year 4 BCE, raised in Rome, and became one of the best-known writers and speakers of his age. Late in life, after years spent advising the emperor Nero, he stepped back from public affairs and began to write long, thoughtful letters on how a person should live. They are known today as the Moral Letters, and they have found readers in almost every century since.

The letters are addressed to Lucilius, a younger friend who served the Roman state and, it seems, governed the island of Sicily. Seneca insists in one letter that he wants his writing to sound like a conversation, plain and unforced, as if the two men were walking side by side. Whatever he teaches, therefore, he teaches gently, as one friend to another and never as a stern master to a pupil.

Seneca belonged to a school of thought called Stoicism, founded in Athens around 300 BCE by Zeno, who taught beneath a painted porch known in Greek as the stoa. Its followers believed that a good life comes from using reason, practising virtue and meeting whatever happens with a steady mind. Seneca's letters turn these grand ideas into practical advice for ordinary mornings and difficult days.

In the very first letter, Seneca urges Lucilius to take hold of his time and to claim it for himself, since time is the one thing that is truly ours. We lose it, he warns, in small unnoticed pieces, through carelessness, through idleness and through busy tasks that matter to nobody. He asks his friend to hold every hour in his grasp, so that he will depend less upon tomorrow.

In the second letter Seneca cautions that a person who is everywhere, as the saying goes, is nowhere, and the same may be said of a reader who skips from book to book. Food cannot nourish the body if it is swallowed and immediately lost, and ideas cannot nourish the mind unless they are digested. He therefore recommends choosing a few trusted writers and returning to them until their thoughts have become part of oneself.

Seneca devotes the third letter to the subject of friendship, and he begins with a warning against both extremes. We should not share our secrets with everyone, he cautions, nor should we refuse to trust anyone at all, since the first is careless and the second is lonely. Think long before you accept a friend, he says, but once you have made the choice, open your heart to him completely.

Death is one of Seneca's favourite subjects, and in the fourth letter he argues that the dread of it can poison an entire life long before the end arrives. Philosophy, he says, teaches us to look at death steadily and to see it as a natural part of being alive. A person who has made peace with it, he believes, is free to enjoy each day without trembling.

Philosophy is not meant to be a performance, Seneca writes in the fifth letter, and a person who wears rough clothes in order to be noticed has missed the point. He advises Lucilius to live differently inside but to look much the same outside, avoiding both luxury and showy poverty. A quiet and modest life, he suggests, is the most convincing advertisement that wisdom can ever have.

In the sixth letter Seneca confesses that he feels himself being not merely improved but transformed, and he longs to pass the benefit on to his friend. He declares that if wisdom were offered to him on condition that he must keep it to himself, he would refuse it, for no good thing is truly pleasant to possess alone. This is the spirit in which every letter is written, as a gift passed from one hand to another.

The seventh letter is a warning about crowds, for Seneca reports that he returns from them more greedy, more ambitious and less kind than when he went in. Faults are contagious, he explains, and a person who stands among many voices slowly begins to repeat them, especially at the cruel public shows that Rome loved. He advises Lucilius to spend his time with people who will make him better, and with those whom he can improve in turn.

The eighth letter tells us why Seneca has stepped away from public life, and the reason is not laziness, since he works harder in retirement than he ever did before. He is writing, he says, for those who will live after him, in the hope that his words may show them the road he wishes he had found sooner. It was a modest ambition when he wrote it down, and it has proved a remarkably successful one over the centuries.

Can a wise person be completely self-sufficient, and if so, why does he need friends? Seneca answers in the ninth letter that the wise man can bear any loss, yet he still seeks companions, not so that someone will nurse him in sickness, but so that he may have someone to care for. Friendship, in his view, is a choice made from fullness rather than from need.

In the twelfth letter Seneca describes a visit to his country house, where the walls are crumbling, the trees are old and he himself has plainly aged along with them. He does not complain, but declares that old age has its own sweetness, like the last fruit of the season, which tastes best because it is nearly gone. Let us go to sleep each night with joy, he says, and be able to say that we have lived.

Seneca observes in the thirteenth letter that there are more things to frighten us than to crush us, and that we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. A fear that grows in the dark of our own thoughts, he suggests, often shrinks when it is examined in the light of the day. Do not run to meet your troubles, he says, for they may never arrive, and if they do, you will meet them then.

Philosophy, Seneca tells his friend in the sixteenth letter, is not a clever trick to be displayed in public, but a daily guide that shapes the mind and steadies the hand. Without it, he claims, no person can live free from fear, because the troubles of life will always seem larger than our resources for meeting them. He asks Lucilius to practise it every day, as one practises a skill that one wishes to master.

The eighteenth letter was written as the festival of Saturnalia approached, a season of feasting and gifts, and Seneca uses it for an unusual experiment. He recommends that Lucilius set aside a few days to live on the plainest food and the roughest clothes, and then to ask himself whether this was really what he feared. The exercise, he promises, takes away the terror of misfortune by showing how little a person needs to survive.

Seneca reminds Lucilius in the twentieth letter that philosophy is meant to teach us how to act, not merely how to speak well. A person whose words and life are at odds, he warns, is like a signpost that points to places it never visits, and nobody should follow it. The test of any teaching, therefore, is the quiet evidence of the way a person behaves when no one is listening.

In the twenty-first letter Seneca makes his friend a promise that might have sounded boastful from anyone else. Just as earlier writers had made their friends famous by writing about them, he says, his own pages will carry the name of Lucilius far into the future. Nearly two thousand years later, the promise has come true, for we still know of Lucilius only because Seneca wrote to him.

Seneca insists in the twenty-third letter that true joy is a serious matter, quite different from the noisy amusements most people chase. It does not depend on money, praise or any lucky event, he says, because it grows from within, out of a calm mind and a clear conscience. A person who has found it carries a quiet cheerfulness wherever he goes, and no one can take it away.

In the twenty-fifth letter, Seneca borrows a piece of advice from the Greek thinker Epicurus, which is to choose a good person and to live as if he were always watching. Such an imagined witness, he suggests, steadies the hand and straightens the conscience, even in a moment when we believe nobody will ever know. His own favourite example was Cato, a Roman famous for his courage and honesty.

Seneca is honest about his own faults in the twenty-seventh letter, and he refuses to pose as a perfectly healthy teacher. He compares himself to a patient who is lying in the same hospital as his friend, and who talks about the illness that they have in common while offering what remedies he has found. The humility of the image is part of its charm, for it turns a lecture into companionship.

In the twenty-eighth letter Seneca addresses a familiar complaint, which is that travel has failed to cure a restless and troubled mind. A change of scenery cannot help, he explains, since we carry ourselves wherever we go, and the burden we meant to leave behind simply comes aboard with us. What we need to change, he says, is not the sky above us but the soul within.

The thirtieth letter paints a gentle portrait of Aufidius Bassus, an old friend of Seneca who was weak with age and illness. Bassus was not frightened of the end, but cheerful, and he spoke of death as a natural change, as one might speak of a journey that is nearly over. Seneca holds him up as an example of what a lifetime of thought can give a person at the last.

Seneca teases Lucilius in the thirty-third letter for sending him so many neat quotations from famous thinkers. Wise sayings are useful, he admits, but a person who only repeats them is like a child who learns his lessons by heart and never begins to understand. He urges his friend to speak for himself, so that what he has found may be recognised as truly his own.

In the thirty-eighth letter Seneca explains why his letters read like conversation, which is that a quiet talk enters the mind far more deeply than a loud speech. Words spoken gently, he says, are like seeds that fall into the soil and wait, so that they sprout in their own time. A few sentences between friends may therefore do more good than a whole afternoon of lectures.

In the forty-seventh letter Seneca turns to the enslaved people who served in Roman households, and he asks his friend to remember that they are human beings like himself. They breathe the same air, he says, and live and die beneath the same sky, so a person should treat those below him as he hopes to be treated by those above. Seneca lived in a society that accepted slavery, and this letter did not call for its end, yet it asks for kindness at a time when many showed none.

Seneca writes in the fifty-first letter about Baiae, the elegant seaside resort near Naples, where wealthy Romans went to enjoy themselves. He decided not to linger there, for a place of constant parties and soft living, he says, makes it harder for a person to remain strong. We should choose our surroundings, he suggests, as carefully as we choose our friends, since both shape the person we become.

In the fifty-third letter Seneca tells a story against himself, describing a short sea voyage on which he became so seasick that he begged to be put ashore. Having recovered, he laughs at his own weakness, but he also draws a lesson from it, which is that no one can mend a fault he has refused to notice. Philosophy, he says, begins when we stop pretending to be stronger than we are.

Seneca suffered for years from a breathing illness, most likely asthma, and in the fifty-fourth letter he describes how it seized him with attacks that felt like a long rehearsal for death. When one of these attacks had passed, he found that he feared nothing, for death, he reasoned, would simply be a return to the state in which he had lain before he was born. Whether or not a reader agrees, the passage shows a man thinking calmly while struggling for breath.

The fifty-sixth letter is one of Seneca's funniest, for it describes his lodgings above a public bathhouse, where athletes grunt, sellers shout and swimmers splash from morning to night. At first he is driven to despair, but he gradually learns to let the noise pass over him, and he concludes that real quiet cannot be found by closing a window. It must be made inside the mind, he says, and a mind that has made it will find silence almost anywhere.

On a journey near Naples, Seneca passed through a long tunnel so dark and so thick with dust that he felt a sudden shock of fear, and he describes the experience in the fifty-seventh letter. Even a philosopher, he admits, cannot prevent the body's first reaction, which comes before the mind has time to reason. What a wise person can do is to notice that reaction and to refuse to be ruled by it a moment later.

When a friend of Lucilius died, Seneca wrote the sixty-third letter to console him, and he does not pretend that grief is wrong. Let the tears fall, he says, but let them also stop, for the memory of a good friend is a gift that should be treasured, not turned into endless sorrow. We honour those we have lost, he suggests, by remembering them with thanks for the time we were given.

If a sailor does not know which harbour he is heading for, Seneca says in the seventy-first letter, no wind will ever seem to be the right one. The same is true of a life, which drifts at the mercy of every breeze unless its owner has decided what he is steering towards. For the Stoics, the harbour was a good character, and every day was a chance to sail a little closer to it.

In the seventy-sixth letter Seneca admits, with a smile, that despite his age he has been attending the lectures of a philosopher called Metronax, and that neighbours find the sight comical. He answers that there is no shame in learning as long as one lives, since the art of living well is the hardest and the longest of all studies. To begin late, he says, is far better than never to begin at all, and no age is too advanced for such a beginning.

In the seventy-seventh letter Seneca stands among a crowd of people watching ships arrive from Egypt, and the scene sets him thinking about the voyage of life. A life, he says, is like a play, in which the length of the performance is far less important than the skill with which each part is acted. It is better to be remembered for a short life lived well than to have dragged out a long one without purpose.

Seneca had known illness all his life, and in the seventy-eighth letter he writes about pain with the authority of a man who has lived with it. A calm mind, he says, does not remove suffering, but it can keep it from growing larger than it needs to be, and happy memories and good company often lighten what remains. It is not a medical teaching, of course, but a way of keeping the spirit steady while the body is unwell.

Seneca returns to the question of reading in the eighty-fourth letter, and this time he compares a good reader to a bee, which visits many flowers and gathers a little from each. Back at the hive the bee transforms what it has collected into honey, and in the same way a reader must blend what he has learned until it becomes something new and his own. The best education, he says, is the kind that leaves no visible trace of the borrowing, because it has become part of the learner.

In the ninety-first letter Seneca reflects on a terrible fire that destroyed much of the Roman city of Lyon, in what is now France. One night, he says, lay between a great city and almost none, and the event should remind us how quickly any fortune can change. He does not conclude that we should despair, but that we should hold our possessions lightly and prepare our minds for loss.

The ninety-second letter sets out the Stoic idea of happiness, which is that the gift that makes us human is reason, and that a life guided by reason is the surest road to contentment. Wealth, health and reputation are pleasant, Seneca allows, but none of them can make a person truly happy if his character is poor. Many readers have found this a challenging claim, yet it is the heart of the Stoic view.

In the ninety-fifth letter Seneca argues that human beings are made for one another, and that to harm a fellow person is to act against our own nature. Society is like an arch of stones, he says, which would collapse if each stone did not press against its neighbours and hold them up. Kindness, in this picture, is not a luxury added to life, but the force that keeps the whole structure standing.

Seneca cautions in the ninety-eighth letter that good fortune is a poor foundation, since luck gives freely and takes back just as easily. He advises his friend to enjoy what he has while keeping his mind prepared for change, for a person who has already thought about misfortune is hard to knock down when it arrives. Such preparation is not gloomy, he insists, but a quiet source of steady courage that lasts through both fortune and loss.

The one hundred and first letter begins with the sudden death of a friend who had seemed perfectly healthy, and Seneca uses it as a reminder of how little we control. Since tomorrow is never promised, he says, the sensible course is to arrange each day as though it were a complete life, leaving nothing important unsaid or undone. The thought is not meant to be sad, but to make each ordinary day shine a little more brightly.

The one hundred and fourth letter shows a more tender side of Seneca, who explains that he has been taking care of his health out of love for his wife, Paulina. She worries about him constantly, he says, and he has learned to be gentle with himself because her peace of mind depends upon his. A person who is loved, the letter quietly implies, owes some care to the people who love him.

In the one hundred and seventh letter, Seneca translates into Latin some famous lines by the Stoic Cleanthes, which say that fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling. The picture is vivid, for it shows two travellers going down the same road, one walking with his head high and the other hauled along in complaint. We cannot choose every event, the Stoics taught, but we can choose whether to meet it with grace.

Seneca urges Lucilius in the one hundred and fifteenth letter not to be dazzled by gold, by polished speeches or by any glittering surface. If it were possible to see a good character with our eyes, he says, we would find it so beautiful that all the jewels in the world would look dull beside it. True value, in his view, lies where the eye cannot reach, in honesty, courage and a gentle heart.

In the one hundred and nineteenth letter Seneca argues that nature asks very little of us, and that the greater part of our worries come from wants that nature never demanded. Bread, water and a roof are enough to keep a person alive, he says, and everything beyond these is a kind of decoration. The person who learns to want only what he needs, he concludes, has already become rich.

The last of the letters that survive, number one hundred and twenty-four, returns to the question that has run through the whole collection, which is where the true good is to be found. Animals follow pleasure, says Seneca, but human beings have been given reason, and it is by reason that we grasp what is truly worth having. He ends by asking his friend to keep using that gift every day, with patience and with care.

In the year 65, after a plot against the emperor Nero was uncovered, Seneca was accused of belonging to it, although historians doubt that he truly took part. Nero ordered him to end his own life, and the historian Tacitus reports that Seneca received the order calmly and tried to comfort his weeping friends by reminding them of the lessons of philosophy. His death, as Tacitus tells it, was the last practical test of everything he had written.

After Seneca's death, his letters were copied by hand for centuries, admired by early Christian writers and read with enthusiasm in the Renaissance, when the French thinker Montaigne drew upon them freely. Today they are available in many languages, and a new generation of readers has turned to them for help with stress, loss and the endless busyness of modern life. Their durability suggests that the questions Seneca asked are simply the questions that people never stop asking.

Seneca did not write to be admired, but to help a friend live a little better, and his advice can be gathered into a handful of daily habits. Guard your time, choose your companions with care, meet your fears with a clear head, be kind to everyone you meet, and begin now rather than waiting for a perfect moment. Choose one of these letters to try today, and, as Seneca might say, you will already have begun.
